content:
I recently noticed that Apple seems to have abandoned Cinematic Mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my disappointment with this.

It's not because the feature is bad, but because it's so close to being genuinely usable, making it even harder to understand why Apple didn't take advantage of the massive performance improvements between its debut on the iPhone 13 and the latest iPhone. Let me show you…

I've previously explained why I understand Apple not prioritising updates to this feature, but at the same time I believe Apple should do so, so it can encourage future videographers and filmmakers — especially young people who may not have access to other camera equipment.

I have a friend who likes conducting street interviews with strangers using his smartphone, often getting them to say things you wouldn't expect. I decided to turn things around, have him sit on a bench, and film him with a smartphone — my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to see how complex a scene Cinematic Mode could handle: one person sitting in the foreground, with railings about 25 feet behind him, and the O2 Arena perhaps close to a thousand feet further beyond across the river. Plus, since he'd be sitting on a bench, his range of movement would be very limited.

The answer is… very close, but not quite there yet. The overall effect is decent, but there's a noticeable halo issue between CK's legs and the railings, and when he moves his head past the support structures of the O2, those structures sometimes become sharp. When he opens both arms, the river behind sometimes suddenly becomes sharp as well:

To be fair, CK felt that the average viewer watching this footage probably wouldn't notice the issue. If they're not a filmmaker or a tech enthusiast familiar with how the feature works, they might not notice these flaws at all — and even if they did, they wouldn't find them bothersome. I assume he might be right.

But the issue really bugs me, and I think even amateur filmmaking enthusiasts would share the same disappointment — and these people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the beginning, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I genuinely believe that if Apple made good use of the processing power and neural capabilities of current iPhone chips, this feature could be dramatically improved. In fact, I'd expect a properly updated Cinematic Mode to handle far more complex scenes than just this one.

Do you agree with my view? Do you want Apple to take Cinematic Mode seriously? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
